mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180 CDI engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A replacement engine for an A180 CDI typically costs between £600 and £4,800 depending on the engine code and condition. Used OM607 units start from £600-£1,500, reconditioned from £1,800-£3,200, and fully rebuilt OM651 engines from £2,500-£4,800. Labour for supply & fit adds £400-£800.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of timing chain failure in a Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: On OM651-equipped A180 CDI models (2012-2014), the most common symptom is a rattling noise from the rear of the engine on cold start. Other signs include loss of power, engine misfires, and the engine management light illuminating. If you hear any unusual sounds, have the timing system inspected immediately - ignoring the rattle can lead to catastrophic engine failure.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the generation and condition. A W169 A180 CDI is typically worth £1,500-£4,000 - a full engine replacement often exceeds the car's value, making a used engine or targeted repair more economical. A W176 A180 CDI is worth £4,000-£12,000 - a rebuilt OM651 or OM607 engine (£2,200-£4,800) can be a worthwhile investment if you plan to keep the car.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180 CDI engine last?

acceptedAnswer.text: The OM640 (W169) and OM651 (early W176) engines are known for their durability and can exceed 200,000-250,000 miles with proper maintenance. The OM607 (late W176) is also capable of high mileage, but its timing belt must be replaced every 80,000-100,000 miles - failure to do so is catastrophic.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the OM651 and OM607 engines in the A180 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: The OM651 is Mercedes' own 1.8-litre four-cylinder diesel with a rear-mounted timing chain, used in the W176 A180 CDI from 2012-2014. The OM607 is a Renault-sourced 1.5-litre diesel (K9K) with a timing belt, introduced in the 2014 facelift and used until 2018. Both produce 109 hp, but the OM651 has more torque (250 Nm vs 260 Nm). The OM607 is lighter and more fuel-efficient, but its timing belt requires regular replacement.

mainEntity.name: What causes the Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180 CDI to lose power?

acceptedAnswer.text: Power loss in the A180 CDI can be caused by several issues depending on the engine. On OM651 engines, timing chain stretch can cause cam timing drift, reducing power. On both OM651 and OM607, EGR valve clogging, DPF blockage, or turbocharger actuator failure are common culprits. On OM607, a failing timing belt can also cause timing drift.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180 CDI - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The 180 CDI badge arrived with the second-generation W169 A-Class in 2004, using Mercedes' own 2.0-litre OM640 diesel producing 109 hp. It was replaced in 2012 by the W176-generation A180 CDI, which initially used the 1.8-litre OM651 before switching to a Renault-sourced 1.5-litre OM607 in 2014. The badge continued into the W177 generation as the A180d, marking the end of the "CDI" naming.

milestones.description: OM640 DE 20 LA (640.940), 2.0L diesel, 109 hp - W169 A180 CDI launch; Mercedes' own four-cylinder common-rail diesel
Facelift with revised engine management; power remains 109 hp; BlueEFFICIENCY tweaks introduced
OM651 DE 18 (651.901), 1.8L diesel, 109 hp - W176 A180 CDI launch; rear-mounted timing chain design
OM607 DE 15 (607.951), 1.5L diesel, 109 hp - W176 A180 CDI switches to Renault-sourced 1.5 dCi engine; timing belt instead of chain
W177 generation launches; "180 CDI" badge replaced by "A180d" with OM607 1.5L diesel continuing

historyTimeline.closingNote: Every engine fitted to the Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180 CDI is covered below, with UK rebuilt pricing and known failure points.

commonProblems.h2: Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180 CDI Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The A180 CDI has been powered by three different diesel engines across its production life - the robust OM640 (W169), the torque-rich OM651 (early W176), and the Renault-sourced OM607 (late W176). Each has distinct failure patterns. Rebuilt A180 CDI engines through EnginesMarket include upgraded components addressing the original failure points, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: OM651 Timing Chain Tensioner Failure - Why the Early W176 A180 CDI Rattles on Cold Start
problems.rootCause: The OM651 uses a single timing chain located at the rear of the engine near the gearbox. The plastic chain tensioner guides wear prematurely and the hydraulic tensioner can lose pressure, allowing chain stretch and camshaft timing drift. Cold-start rattle is the classic warning sign.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace timing chain, tensioner, guides, sprockets
repairOptions.longevity: Best done at first rattle; prevents catastrophic failure

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit rebuilt OM651 with upgraded timing components
repairOptions.longevity: Required if chain has jumped; bent valves almost certain

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical W176 A180 CDI is worth £4,000-£12,000 depending on condition and mileage. For vehicles under £5,000, a preventative chain replacement (£1,400-£2,200) is usually the better financial decision than a full engine replacement. For higher-value examples, a rebuilt OM651 with warranty (£2,500-£4,800) offers peace of mind.
problems.recommendation: If you hear a rattling noise from the rear of the engine on cold starts - especially between 80,000 and 120,000 miles - act immediately. A preventative chain replacement at a specialist saves thousands compared to waiting for failure. Once the chain jumps, piston-to-valve contact is almost certain and engine replacement becomes the only viable option.

problems.h4: OM607 Timing Belt Failure - The Renault-Sourced Engine's Critical Weak Point
problems.rootCause: The OM607 is a Renault K9K-sourced engine that uses a timing belt rather than a chain. The belt must be replaced every 80,000-100,000 miles - failure causes piston-to-valve contact and complete engine destruction.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace timing belt, tensioner, water pump
repairOptions.longevity: Essential maintenance; do not exceed 100k miles

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit rebuilt engine with new belt and tensioner
repairOptions.longevity: Required if belt has snapped; valves and pistons damaged

problems.recommendation: Unlike the OM651, the OM607's timing belt failure is predictable and preventable. If your OM607-equipped A180 CDI is approaching 80,000 miles or 5 years since the last belt change, replace it immediately. A £350-£650 specialist belt change is far cheaper than a £2,200+ engine replacement.

problems.group: OM651 & OM607 EGR Cooler & Injector Issues
problems.h4: OM651 & OM607 EGR Cooler & Injector Issues - Diesel Common-Rail Weaknesses
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz A-Class 180 CDI (OM651.901 and OM607.951, W176, 2012-2018)
problems.rootCause: The EGR cooler on OM651 engines develops micro-cracks due to thermal cycling, leaking coolant into the exhaust. Injector seal failure is common on both OM651 and OM607, causing combustion gas blow-by and poor cold starting.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace EGR cooler, flush cooling system
repairOptions.longevity: Viable if caught early before engine damage

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove injectors, replace seals and bolts
repairOptions.longevity: Viable if injectors are not seized

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete engine with upgraded EGR and new injector seals
repairOptions.longevity: Required if coolant ingestion has bent a rod

problems.recommendation: White smoke on startup, a "sweet" exhaust smell, and frequent low coolant warnings are early warning signs of EGR cooler failure. Replace the EGR cooler at the first symptom - a £500 specialist repair beats a £2,500 replacement engine.
